clinicalPearls: The condition causes progressive atrophy of the skin, subcutaneous fat, muscle, and sometimes underlying bone and cartilage on one side of the face
It is regarded as lying on the spectrum of localised scleroderma and overlaps clinically with linear scleroderma of the 'en coup de sabre' type
Onset is usually in the first two decades of life, with an active phase of variable duration followed by stabilisation, leaving a characteristic facial asymmetry
Neurological complications, including seizures, migraine, and focal deficits, can occur, sometimes with ipsilateral brain imaging abnormalities
Ophthalmological involvement such as enophthalmos, uveitis, and extraocular changes may accompany the facial atrophy
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging to define the extent of tissue loss and to screen for intracranial involvement
Immunomodulatory therapy may be used during the active inflammatory phase, while reconstructive procedures such as autologous fat transfer are reserved for the burnt-out, stable stage
reference.pathophysiology: Parry-Romberg syndrome is a progressive hemifacial atrophy considered part of the localised scleroderma spectrum. Although the cause is not fully established, an immune-mediated, inflammatory process is favoured, potentially with neurovascular or trophic contributions, leading to progressive loss of dermal, subcutaneous, muscular, and occasionally osseous tissue confined largely to one side of the face. The inflammatory activity tends to be self-limited over months to years, after which atrophy stabilises, but the accumulated tissue loss produces lasting asymmetry. Its overlap with linear scleroderma 'en coup de sabre' supports a shared sclerodermatous mechanism, and associated central nervous system and ocular findings suggest the process can extend beyond the skin.
additionalDifferentials: Post-traumatic or post-surgical facial soft-tissue loss
Hemifacial microsomia and congenital facial asymmetry
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the face and brain to define soft-tissue and bony atrophy and screen for intracranial involvement
Clinical photography and serial measurement to monitor progression
Dermatological assessment for coexisting sclerodermatous skin changes
Ophthalmological examination for enophthalmos and uveitis
Autoimmune serology where an inflammatory or connective tissue process is being evaluated
redFlags: New seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting intracranial involvement
Rapidly progressive tissue loss during an active inflammatory phase
Ocular inflammation or visual disturbance requiring ophthalmology input
Involvement crossing to bone and cartilage with functional impairment of the eye, mouth, or airway
reference.prognosis: The disease typically progresses over a period of years and then stabilises, leaving fixed facial asymmetry of variable severity. Prognosis for function is generally good once the active phase resolves, though neurological or ocular complications can cause lasting morbidity, and reconstructive surgery in the stable phase can substantially improve appearance.
pitfalls: Mistaking early atrophy for weight loss or benign asymmetry and missing the active, treatable inflammatory phase
Undertaking reconstructive surgery before the disease has stabilised, risking continued atrophy
Overlooking associated neurological or ocular disease that requires specific management
Failing to recognise the overlap with localised scleroderma and its implications for systemic assessment
management: Suppress the active inflammatory phase with immunosuppression such as methotrexate, often combined with systemic corticosteroids as used in localised scleroderma, with mycophenolate mofetil as an alternative
Monitor disease activity with serial clinical photography, measurement, and MRI to judge progression and treatment response
Defer reconstructive surgery such as autologous fat grafting or free-tissue transfer until the atrophic process has stabilised
Treat neurological complications, using anticonvulsants for seizures and appropriate prophylaxis for migraine
Refer for ophthalmological management of uveitis and other ocular involvement with anti-inflammatory therapy
Coordinate care across dermatology, plastic surgery, neurology, and ophthalmology
